high.title: Exported component consumes attacker-controlled Intent data
high.description:
3 findings in this app combine into one exploitable path: "Exported activity UserDetailsActivity has no permission protection", "Permission bypass via exported activity granting URI permissions" and "The exported UserDetailsActivity performs a permission bypass by taking".

Attack path:
1. Attacker app starts UserDetailsActivity (AndroidManifest.xml)
2. Attacker app provides a 'path' extra in the Intent
3. UserDetailsActivity (UserDetailsActivity.java) reads the 'path' extra
4. UserDetailsActivity constructs a URI for UserDetailsContentProvider
5. UserDetailsActivity returns the URI via setResult with FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION
6. Attacker app uses the returned URI to query UserDetailsContentProvider
high.impact: The component is invokable by any app on the device and acts on the Intent it is handed without validating it, so a malicious app drives the target app's privileged behaviour with data of its choosing.
high.recommendation: Guard the component with a signature-level permission, or unexport it. Validate every Intent extra before use, and never forward a nested Intent received from a caller.

high.title: Permission bypass via exported activity granting URI permissions
high.description: UserDetailsActivity is exported and accepts a 'path' extra from an incoming Intent, which it uses to construct a URI for the UserDetailsContentProvider. It then returns this URI via setResult() with FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION (1), bypassing the 'signature' permission guarding the provider.
high.impact: An unprivileged third-party app can obtain read access to sensitive user data (including SSNs and addresses) by requesting specific paths through the exported activity.

lines_html: protected void onResume() {
super.onResume();
android.content.Intent recvIntent = getIntent();
java.lang.String path = recvIntent.getStringExtra("path");
android.net.Uri uri = android.net.Uri.parse("content://edu.ksu.cs.benign.userdetails" + path);
android.content.Intent sendIntent = new android.content.Intent();
sendIntent.setFlags(1);
sendIntent.setData(uri);
setResult(RES_CODE, sendIntent);

high.recommendation: Avoid granting URI permissions to arbitrary paths provided by external Intents. Validate the 'path' input against a strict allowlist or remove the exported activity.

info.description: android:debuggable="true" lets any user with adb attach a debugger to the process, read and modify memory, and inspect application data. The application is marked as debuggable (android:debuggable="true"), which enables the JDWP debugger and allows the use of 'run-as' to access the app's private data directory.
info.impact: An attacker with local access can inspect the app's memory, modify its state at runtime, and extract sensitive files from the internal sandbox.
info.recommendation: Remove android:debuggable or set it to "false" for release builds.

reasons: Debuggable release build. A debuggable build is a release-pipeline defect rather than an exploitable flaw - attaching a debugger already requires ADB access to the device. Worth fixing, not worth a severity.

info.title: Lack of screenshot protection
info.description: The application does not set FLAG_SECURE on any of its activities, allowing the system and other apps to capture screenshots or recordings of the app's UI.
info.impact: Sensitive information displayed on the screen (such as user details or SSNs) can be captured and leaked through screenshots or the recents screen thumbnail.
info.recommendation: Apply Window.setFlags(WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE) to activities displaying sensitive data.

reasons: Screen contents not protected from capture. Without FLAG_SECURE, what a screen shows can end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview. That matters on screens showing credentials, card numbers or balances; on its own it is a hardening note.

info.title: No network security config declared
info.description: The app declares neither android:networkSecurityConfig nor usesCleartextTraffic, so it relies on platform defaults and pins no domain. With targetSdkVersion 27 those defaults still permit cleartext HTTP (see the cleartext finding).
info.impact: Without pinning, anyone who gets a CA trusted on the device can read and alter the app's TLS traffic.
info.recommendation: Declare a network security config that disables cleartext and pins the domains that carry sensitive traffic.

reasons: No certificate pinning. Pinning defends against an attacker who already controls a trusted CA or the device's trust store. Without one of those, TLS is still doing its job. It becomes a finding when paired with what the unpinned channel actually carries.
Requires evidence of sensitive data being sent over an unpinned channel.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 allows implicit component export
info.description: On targetSdk 27, any component with an intent-filter is exported unless it says otherwise.
info.recommendation: Raise targetSdkVersion to 31+ and declare android:exported explicitly on every filtered component.

reasons: Legacy platform behaviour from SDK levels. An SDK level is a statement about which platform defaults apply, not a defect. It is context for the findings that depend on those defaults - pair it with one of them.
This is a platform default that provides context for other findings.
warnings: Implicit export only applies below targetSdk 31; confirm the app's targetSdkVersion before treating this as exploitable.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 permits cleartext traffic by default
info.description: targetSdk 27 predates API 28, where cleartext HTTP became opt-in. The app targets SDK 27 (targetSdkVersion="27") and does not define a Network Security Configuration, which permits cleartext (HTTP) traffic by default.
info.impact: Sensitive data transmitted over HTTP can be intercepted or modified via man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks.

reasons: Cleartext permitted by configuration. The flag permits HTTP; it does not show that anything is sent over it. Name a request that actually goes out in cleartext, and what it carries, and this is a genuine finding.
Requires a demonstrated HTTP request to establish impact.
warnings: Cleartext is blocked by default from targetSdk 28; confirm the declared target and any network security config.

info.title: Task hijacking (StrandHogg) possible on Android 10 and lower
info.description: minSdkVersion 22 lets the app run on Android versions before 11, and its task affinity is its package name "edu.ksu.cs.benign". There, another app can declare the same affinity, with allowTaskReparenting, and have its own activity shown in this app's task. The application targets SDK 27 and does not specify an empty taskAffinity for its activities. This allows a malicious app with the same affinity to potentially slide its own activities into the victim's task stack.
info.impact: An attacker can perform a phishing attack by overlaying a fake login or data-entry screen over the legitimate app's task.
info.recommendation: Raise minSdkVersion to 30, where Android fixed this. Until then, android:taskAffinity="" on the <application> mitigates the original attack, though not its runtime variant on unpatched Android 9 and lower.

info.title: The exported UserDetailsActivity performs a permission bypass by taking
info.description: The exported UserDetailsActivity performs a permission bypass by taking a user-supplied 'path' extra, constructing a content URI for the signature-protected UserDetailsContentProvider, and returning it via setResult with FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION (flag 1). An external app can start this activity with a path like '/user/ssn' to obtain a read-permissioned URI, allowing it to query the provider and steal sensitive user data (including SSNs) despite lacking the required 'edu.ksu.cs.benign.permission.internalRead' signature permission.
